senses.d: To care; to desire.
q: I kepe not of armes for to yelp .

senses.d: To hold; to restrain from departure or removal; not to let go of; to retain in one's power or possession; not to lose; to retain; to detain.
q: If we lose the field, We can not keep the town.
That I may know what keeps me here with you.
If we would weigh and keep in our minds what we are considering, that would instruct us.

senses.d: To cause to remain in a given situation or condition; to maintain unchanged; to hold or preserve in any state or tenor.
q: His loyalty he kept, his love, his zeal.
Keep a stiff rein, and move but gently on.

senses.d: To have in custody; to have in some place for preservation; to take charge of.
q: The crown of Stephanus, first king of Hungary, was always kept in the castle of Vicegrade.

senses.d: To preserve from danger, harm, or loss; to guard.
q: Behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee.

senses.d: To preserve from discovery or publicity; not to communicate, reveal, or betray, as a secret.
q: Great are thy virtues . . . though kept from man.

senses.d: To attend upon; to have the care of; to tend.
q: And the Lord God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden, to dress it and to keep it.
In her girlish age, she kept sheep on the moor.

senses.d: To record transactions, accounts, or events in; as, to keep books, a journal, etc.; also, to enter (as accounts, records, etc. ) in a book.
To maintain, as an establishment, institution, or the like; to conduct; to manage; as, to keep store.
q: Like a pedant that keeps a school.
Every one of them kept house by himself.

senses.d: To supply with necessaries of life; to entertain; as, to keep boarders.
To have in one's service; to have and maintain, as an assistant, a servant, a mistress, a horse, etc.
q: I keep but three men and a boy.

senses.d: To have habitually in stock for sale.

Keep.syn: To retain; detain; reserve; preserve; hold; restrain; maintain; sustain; support; withhold.
Keep.etym: [OE. kēpen, AS. cēpan to keep, regard, desire, await, take, betake; cf. AS. copenere lover, OE. copnien to desire.]

senses.d: To remain in any position or state; to continue; to abide; to stay; as, to keep at a distance; to keep aloft; to keep near; to keep in the house; to keep before or behind; to keep in favor; to keep out of company, or out reach.
To last; to endure; to remain unimpaired.
q: If the malt be not thoroughly dried, the ale it makes will not keep.

senses.d: To reside for a time; to lodge; to dwell.
q: Knock at his study, where, they say, he keeps.

senses.d: To take care; to be solicitous; to watch.
q: Keep that the lusts choke not the word of God that is in us.

senses.d: To be in session; as, school keeps to-day.
The act or office of keeping; custody; guard; care; heed; charge.
q: Pan, thou god of shepherds all, Which of our tender lambkins takest keep.

senses.d: The state of being kept; hence, the resulting condition; case; as, to be in good keep.
The means or provisions by which one is kept; maintenance; support; as, the keep of a horse.
q: Grass equal to the keep of seven cows.
I performed some services to the college in return for my keep.

senses.d: That which keeps or protects; a stronghold; a fortress; a castle; specifically, the strongest and securest part of a castle, often used as a place of residence by the lord of the castle, especially during a siege; the donjon. See Illust. of Castle.
q: The prison strong, Within whose keep the captive knights were laid.
The lower chambers of those gloomy keeps.
I think . . . the keep, or principal part of a castle, was so called because the lord and his domestic circle kept, abode, or lived there.

senses.d: That which is kept in charge; a charge.
q: Often he used of his keep A sacrifice to bring.

senses.d: A cap for retaining anything, as a journal box, in place.
One who, or that which, keeps; one who, or that which, holds or has possession of anything.
One who retains in custody; one who has the care of a prison and the charge of prisoners.
One who has the care, custody, or superintendence of anything; as, the keeper of a park, a pound, of sheep, of a gate, etc.; the keeper of attached property;
q: The Lord is thy keeper.

senses.d: One who remains or keeps in a place or position.
q: Discreet; chaste; keepers at home.

senses.d: A ring, strap, clamp, or any device for holding an object in place; as: (a) The box on a door jamb into which the bolt of a lock protrudes, when shot. (b) A ring serving to keep another ring on the finger. (c) A loop near the buckle of a strap to receive the end of the strap.
A fruit that keeps well; as, the Roxbury Russet is a good keeper.
A holding; restraint; custody; guard; charge; care; preservation.
q: His happiness is in his own keeping.

senses.d: Maintenance; support; provision; feed; as, the cattle have good keeping.
q: The work of many hands, which earns my keeping.

senses.d: Conformity; congruity; harmony; consistency; as, these subjects are in keeping with each other.
Harmony or correspondence between the different parts of a work of art; as, the foreground of this painting is not in keeping.
of Keep.

A square of fine linen worn by women as a covering for the head; hence, anything similar in form or material, worn for ornament on other parts of the person; — mostly used in compounds; as, neckerchief; breastkerchief; and later, handkerchief.
q: He might put on a hat, a muffler, and a kerchief, and so escape.
Her black hair strained away To a scarlet kerchief caught beneath her chin.

senses.d: A lady who wears a kerchief.

Kerchief.etym: [OE. coverchef, OF. cuevrechief, couvrechef, F. couvrechef, a head covering, fr. couvrir to cover + OF. chief head, F. chef. See Cover, Chief, and cf. Curfew.]

senses.d: The essential part of a seed; all that is within the seed walls; the edible substance contained in the shell of a nut; hence, anything included in a shell, husk, or integument; as, the kernel of a nut. See Illust. of Endocarp.
q: ' A were as good crack a fusty nut with no kernel

senses.d: A single seed or grain; as, a kernel of corn.
A small mass around which other matter is concreted; a nucleus; a concretion or hard lump in the flesh.
The central, substantial or essential part of anything; the gist; the core; as, the kernel of an argument.

Kernel.etym: [OE. kernel, kirnel, curnel, AS. cyrnel, fr. corn grain. See Corn, and cf. Kern to harden.]

senses.d: To harden or ripen into kernels; to produce kernels.
A metallic vessel, with a wide mouth, often without a cover, used for heating and boiling water or other liguids.

Kettle.etym: [OE. ketel; cf. AS. cetel, cetil, cytel; akin to D. kjedel, G. kessel, OHG. chezzil, Icel. ketill, SW. kittel, Dan. kjedel, Goth. katils; all perh. fr. L. catillus, dim. of catinus a deep vessel, bowl; but cf. also OHG. chezzī kettle, Icel. kati small ship.]

senses.d: An instrument by means of which the bolt of a lock is shot or drawn; usually, a removable metal instrument fitted to the mechanism of a particular lock and operated by turning in its place.
An instrument which is turned like a key in fastening or adjusting any mechanism; as, a watch key; a bed key, etc.
That part of an instrument or machine which serves as the means of operating it; as, a telegraph key; the keys of a pianoforte, or of a typewriter.

A position or condition which affords entrance, control, pr possession, etc.; as, the key of a line of defense; the key of a country; the key of a political situation. Hence, that which serves to unlock, open, discover, or solve something unknown or difficult; as, the key to a riddle; the key to a problem.
q: Those who are accustomed to reason have got the true key of books.
Who keeps the keys of all the creeds.

senses.d: That part of a mechanism which serves to lock up, make fast, or adjust to position.
A piece of wood used as a wedge.
A keystone.
A wedge to unite two or more pieces, or adjust their relative position; a cotter; a forelock.
An indehiscent, one-seeded fruit furnished with a wing, as the fruit of the ash and maple; a samara; — called also key fruit.

A family of tones whose regular members are called diatonic tones, and named key tone (or tonic) or one (or eight), mediant or three, dominant or five, subdominant or four, submediant or six, supertonic or two, and subtonic or seven. Chromatic tones are temporary members of a key, under such names as “ sharp four, ” “flat seven,” etc. Scales and tunes of every variety are made from the tones of a key.
q: Both warbling of one song, both in one key.

senses.d: Fig: The general pitch or tone of a sentence or utterance.
q: You fall at once into a lower key.

senses.d: To fasten or secure firmly; to fasten or tighten with keys or wedges.
A metallic lever by which the circuit of the sending or transmitting part of a station equipment may be easily and rapidly opened and closed; any device for closing or opening an electric circuit.

A simplified version or analysis which accompanies something as a clue to its explanation, a book or table containing the solutions to problems, ciphers, allegories, or the like, or a table or synopsis of conspicuous distinguishing characters of members of a taxonomic group.
To strike, thrust, or hit violently with the foot; as, a horse kicks a groom; a man kicks a dog.
q: He kicked the shins of his judges.

senses.d: To thrust out the foot or feet with violence; to strike out with the foot or feet, as in defense or in bad temper; esp., to strike backward, as a horse does, or to have a habit of doing so. Hence, figuratively: To show ugly resistance, opposition, or hostility; to spurn.
q: I should kick, being kicked.

senses.d: To recoil; — said of a musket, cannon, etc.
A blow with the foot or feet; a striking or thrust with the foot.
q: A kick, that scarce would move a horse, May kill a sound divine.

senses.d: The projection on the tang of the blade of a pocket knife, which prevents the edge of the blade from striking the spring. See Illust. of Pocketknife.
A projection in a mold, to form a depression in the surface of the brick.
The recoil of a musket or other firearm, when discharged.
A young goat.
q: The . . . leopard shall lie down with the kid.

senses.d: A young child or infant; hence, a simple person, easily imposed on.
A kind of leather made of the skin of the young goat, or of the skin of rats, etc.
Gloves made of kid.
A small wooden mess tub; — a name given by sailors to one in which they receive their food.

Kid.etym: [Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. kið, Dan. & Sw. kid; akin to OHG. kizzi, G. kitz, kitzchen, kitzlein.]

senses.d: To bring forth a young goat.
A fagot; a bundle of heath and furze.
of Kythe.
Among pugilists, thieves, etc., a youthful expert; — chiefly used attributively; as, kid Jones.
A glandular organ which excretes urea and other waste products from the animal body; a urinary gland.
Habit; disposition; sort; kind.
q: There are in later times other decrees, made by popes of another kidney.
Millions in the world of this man's kidney.
Your poets, spendthrifts, and other fools of that kidney, pretend, forsooth, to crack their jokes on prudence.

senses.d: A waiter.

Kidney.etym: [OE. kidnei, kidnere, from Icel. koiðr belly, womb (akin to Goth. gipus, AS. cwiþ womb) + OE. nere kidney; akin to D. nier, G. niere, OHG. nioro, Icel. nȳra, Dan. nyre, Sw. njure, and probably to Gr. νεφρόσ Cf. Kite belly.]

senses.d: A kiln.
A channel or arm of the sea; a river; a stream; as, the channel between Staten Island and Bergen Neck is the Kill van Kull, or the Kills; — used also in composition; as, Schuylkill, Catskill, etc.
To deprive of life, animal or vegetable, in any manner or by any means; to render inanimate; to put to death; to slay.
q: Ah, kill me with thy weapon, not with words !

senses.d: To destroy; to ruin; as, to kill one's chances; to kill the sale of a book.
q: Her lively color kill'd with deadly cares.

senses.d: To cause to cease; to quell; to calm; to still; as, in seamen's language, a shower of rain kills the wind.
q: Be comforted, good madam; the great rage, You see, is killed in him.

senses.d: To destroy the effect of; to counteract; to neutralize; as, alkali kills acid.

Kill.syn: To murder; assassinate; slay; butcher; destroy. — To Kill, Murder, Assassinate. To kill does not necessarily mean any more than to deprive of life. A man may kill another by accident or in self-defense, without the imputation of guilt. To murder is to kill with malicious forethought and intention. To assassinate is to murder suddenly and by stealth. The sheriff may kill without murdering; the duelist murders, but does not assassinate his antagonist; the assassin kills and murders.
Kill.etym: [OE. killen, kellen, cullen, to kill, strike; perh. the same word as cwellen, quellen, to kill (cf. Quell), or perh. rather akin to Icel. kolla to hit in the head, harm, kollr top, summit, head, Sw. kulle, D. kollen to kill with the ax.]

senses.d: The act of killing.
q: “There is none like to me!” says the cub in the pride of his earliest kill.

senses.d: An animal killed in the hunt, as by a beast of prey.
q: If ye plunder his kill from a weaker, devour not all in thy pride.

senses.d: Literally, that kills; having power to kill; fatal; in a colloquial sense, conquering; captivating; irresistible.
q: Those eyes are made so killing.
Nothing could be more killingly spoken.

senses.d: A primitive Chinese instrument of the cittern kind, with from five to twenty-five silken strings.
Relationship, consanguinity, or affinity; connection by birth or marriage; kindred; near connection or alliance, as of those having common descent.
Relatives; persons of the same family or race.
q: The father, mother, and the kin beside.
You are of kin, and so a friend to their persons.

Kin.etym: [OE. kin, cun, AS. cynn kin, kind, race, people; akin to cennan to beget, D. kunne sex, OS. & OHG. kunni kin, race, Icel. kyn, Goth. kuni, G. & D. kind a child, L. genus kind, race, L. gignere to beget, Gr. γίγνεσθαι to be born, Skr. jan to beget. √44. Cf. Kind, King, Gender kind, Nation.]

senses.d: Of the same nature or kind; kinder.
The unit velocity in the C.G.S. system — a velocity of one centimeter per second.
Characteristic of the species; belonging to one's nature; natural; native.
q: It becometh sweeter than it should be, and loseth the kind taste.

senses.d: Having feelings befitting our common nature; congenial; sympathetic; as, a kind man; a kind heart.
q: Yet was he kind, or if severe in aught, The love he bore to learning was his fault.

senses.d: Showing tenderness or goodness; disposed to do good and confer happiness; averse to hurting or paining; benevolent; benignant; gracious.
q: He is kind unto the unthankful and to evil.
O cruel Death, to those you take more kind Than to the wretched mortals left behind.
A fellow feeling makes one wondrous kind.

senses.d: Proceeding from, or characterized by, goodness, gentleness, or benevolence; as, a kind act.
Gentle; tractable; easily governed; as, a horse kind in harness.

Kind.syn: Benevolent; benign; beneficent; bounteous; gracious; propitious; generous; forbearing; indulgent; tender; humane; compassionate; good; lenient; clement; mild; gentle; bland; obliging; friendly; amicable. See Obliging.
Kind.etym: [AS. cynde, gecynde, natural, innate, prop. an old p. p. from the root of E. kin. See Kin kindred.]

senses.d: Nature; natural instinct or disposition.
q: He knew by kind and by no other lore.
Some of you, on pure instinct of nature, Are led by kind t'admire your fellow-creature.

senses.d: Race; genus; species; generic class; as, in mankind or humankind.
q: Every kind of beasts, and of birds.
She follows the law of her kind.
Here to sow the seed of bread, That man and all the kinds be fed.

senses.d: Nature; style; character; sort; fashion; manner; variety; description; class; as, there are several kinds of eloquence, of style, and of music; many kinds of government; various kinds of soil, etc.
q: How diversely Love doth his pageants play, And snows his power in variable kinds !
There is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.
Diogenes was asked in a kind of scorn: What was the matter that philosophers haunted rich men, and not rich men philosophers ?
Tax on tillage was often levied in kind upon corn.

Kind.syn: Sort; species; class; genus; nature; style; character; breed; set.
Kind.etym: [OE. kinde, cunde, AS. cynd. See Kind, a.]

senses.d: To beget.
To bring forth young.
q: The poor beast had but lately kindled.

senses.d: To set on fire; to cause to burn with flame; to ignite; to cause to begin burning; to start; to light; as, to kindle a match, or shavings.
q: His breath kindleth coals.

senses.d: Fig.: To inflame, as the passions; to rouse; to provoke; to excite to action; to heat; to fire; to animate; to incite; as, to kindle anger or wrath; to kindle the flame of love, or love into a flame.
q: So is a contentious man to kindle strife.
Nothing remains but that I kindle the boy thither.
Kindling her undazzled eyes at the full midday beam.
Could swell the soul to rage, or kindle soft desire.

Kindle.syn: Enkindle; light; ignite; inflame; provoke; excite; arouse; stir up.
Kindle.etym: [Icel. kyndill candle, torch; prob. fr. L. candela; cf. also Icel. kynda to kindle. Cf. Candle.]

senses.d: To take fire; to begin to burn with flame; to start as a flame.
q: When thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.

senses.d: Fig.: To begin to be excited; to grow warm or animated; to be roused or exasperated.
q: On all occasions where forbearance might be called for, the Briton kindles, and the Christian gives way.

senses.d: According to the kind or nature; natural.
q: The kindly fruits of the earth.
An herd of bulls whom kindly rage doth sting.
Whatsoever as the Son of God he may do, it is kindly for Him as the Son of Man to save the sons of men.

senses.d: Humane; congenial; sympathetic; hence, disposed to do good to; benevolent; gracious; kind; helpful; as, kindly affections, words, acts, etc.
q: The shade by which my life was crossed, . . . Has made me kindly with my kind.

senses.d: Favorable; mild; gentle; auspicious; beneficent.
q: In soft silence shed the kindly shower.
Should e'er a kindlier time ensue.

senses.d: Naturally; fitly.
q: Examine how kindly the Hebrew manners of speech mix and incorporate with the English language

senses.d: In a kind manner; congenially; with good will; with a disposition to make others happy, or to oblige.
q: Be kindly affectioned one to another, with brotherly love.

senses.d: The state or quality of being kind, in any of its various senses; manifestation of kind feeling or disposition beneficence.
q: I do fear thy nature; It is too full o' the milk of human kindness To catch the nearest way.
Unremembered acts Of kindness and of love.

senses.d: A kind act; an act of good will; as, to do a great kindness.

Kindness.syn: Good will; benignity; grace; tenderness; compassion; humanity; clemency; mildness; gentleness; goodness; generosity; beneficence; favor.

senses.d: Relationship by birth or marriage; consanguinity; affinity; kin.
q: Like her, of equal kindred to the throne.

senses.d: Relatives by blood or marriage, more properly the former; relations; persons related to each other.
q: I think there's no man is secure But the queen's kindred.

Kindred.syn: Kin; kinsfolk; relatives; kinsmen; relations; relationship; affinity.
Kindred.etym: [OE. kinrede, kynrede, kunreden (with excrescent d), fr. AS. cynn kin, race + the termination -rǣden, akin to AS. rǣdan to advise, G. rathen. Cf. Hatred.]

senses.d: Related; congenial; of the like nature or properties; as, kindred souls; kindred skies; kindred propositions.
q: True to the kindred points of heaven and home.

senses.d: Cows.

Kine.etym: [For older kyen, formed like oxen, fr. AS. c�, itself pl. of c� cow. See Cow, and cf. Kee, Kie.]

senses.d: A Chinese musical instrument, consisting of resonant stones or metal plates, arranged according to their tones in a frame of wood, and struck with a hammer.
A chief ruler; a sovereign; one invested with supreme authority over a nation, country, or tribe, usually by hereditary succession; a monarch; a prince.
q: Kings will be tyrants from policy, when subjects are rebels from principle.
There was a State without king or nobles.
But yonder comes the powerful King of Day, Rejoicing in the east

senses.d: One who, or that which, holds a supreme position or rank; a chief among competitors; as, a railroad king; a money king; the king of the lobby; the king of beasts.
A playing card having the picture of a king; as, the king of diamonds.
The chief piece in the game of chess.
A crowned man in the game of draughts.
The title of two historical books in the Old Testament.

King.etym: [AS. cyng, cyning; akin to OS. kuning, D. koning, OHG. kuning, G. könig, Icel. konungr, Sw. konung, Dan. konge; formed with a patronymic ending, and fr. the root of E. kin; cf. Icel. konr a man of noble birth. √44. See Kin.]

senses.d: To supply with a king; to make a king of; to raise to royalty.
q: Those traitorous captains of Israel who kinged themselves by slaying their masters and reigning in their stead.

senses.d: The rank, quality, state, or attributes of a king; royal authority; sovereign power; rule; dominion; monarchy.
q: Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom.
When Jehoram was risen up to the kingdom of his father, he strengthened himself.

senses.d: The territory or country subject to a king or queen; the dominion of a monarch; the sphere in which one is king or has control.
q: Unto the kingdom of perpetual night.
You're welcome, Most learned reverend sir, into our kingdom.

senses.d: An extensive scientific division distinguished by leading or ruling characteristics; a principal division; a department; as, the mineral kingdom.

Kingdom.syn: Realm; empire; dominion; monarchy; sovereignty; domain.

senses.d: Belonging to, suitable to, or becoming, a king; characteristic of, or resembling, a king; directed or administered by a king; monarchical; royal; sovereign; regal; august; noble; grand.
q: The kingliest kings are crowned with thorn.
Leave kingly backs to cope with kingly cares.

Kingly.syn: Regal; royal; monarchical; imperial; august; sovereign; noble; splendid.

senses.d: In a kingly or kinglike manner.
q: Low bowed the rest; he, kingly, did but nod.

senses.d: Relatives; kindred; kin; persons of the same family or closely related families.
q: They sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance.

senses.d: A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.
A female relative.
A workman's name for the graphite which forms incidentally in iron smelting.
To salute with the lips, as a mark of affection, reverence, submission, forgiveness, etc.
q: He . . . kissed her lips with such a clamorous smack, That at the parting all the church echoed.

senses.d: To touch gently, as if fondly or caressingly.
q: When the sweet wind did gently kiss the trees.

Kiss.etym: [OE. kissen, cussen, AS. cyssan, fr. coss a kiss; of uncertain origin; akin to D. kus, G. kuss, Icel. koss.]

senses.d: To make or give salutation with the lips in token of love, respect, etc.; as, kiss and make friends.
To meet; to come in contact; to touch fondly.
q: Like fire and powder, Which as they kiss consume.
Rose, rose and clematis, Trail and twine and clasp and kiss.

senses.d: A salutation with the lips, as a token of affection, respect, etc.; as, a parting kiss; a kiss of reconciliation.
q: Last with a kiss, she took a long farewell.
Dear as remembered kisses after death.

senses.d: A small piece of confectionery.

Kiss.etym: [OE. kiss, derived under the influence of the verb from the older form coss, AS. coss. See Kiss, v.]

senses.d: Any raptorial bird of the subfamily Milvinæ, of which many species are known. They have long wings, adapted for soaring, and usually a forked tail.
Fig. : One who is rapacious.
q: Detested kite, thou liest.

senses.d: A light frame of wood or other material covered with paper or cloth, for flying in the air at the end of a string.
A lofty sail, carried only when the wind is light.
A quadrilateral, one of whose diagonals is an axis of symmetry.

Fictitious commercial paper used for raising money or to sustain credit, as a check which represents no deposit in bank, or a bill of exchange not sanctioned by sale of goods; an accommodation check or bill.
The brill.

Kite.etym: [OE. kyte, AS. cȳta; cf. W. cud, cut.]

senses.d: To raise money by “kites;” as, kiting transactions. See Kite, 6.
The belly.
A form of drag to be towed under water at any depth up to about forty fathoms, which on striking bottom is upset and rises to the surface; — called also sentry.
To work and press into a mass, usually with the hands; esp., to work, as by repeated pressure with the knuckles, into a well mixed mass, as the materials of bread, cake, etc.; as, to knead dough.
q: The kneading, the making of the cake, the heating of the oven, and the baking.

senses.d: Fig.: To treat or form as by kneading; to beat.
q: I will knead him : I'll make him supple.

Knead.etym: [OE. kneden, As. cnedan; akin to D. kneden, G. kneten, Sw. knåda, Icel. knoða; cf. OSlav. gnesti.]

senses.d: In man, the joint in the middle part of the leg.
The joint, or region of the joint, between the thigh and leg.
A piece of timber or metal formed with an angle somewhat in the shape of the human knee when bent.
A bending of the knee, as in respect or courtesy.
q: Give them title, knee, and approbation.

Knee.etym: [OE. kne, cneo, As. cneó, cneów; akin to OS. knio, kneo, OFries. knī, G. & D. knie, OHG. chniu, chneo, Icel. knē, Sw. knä, Dan. knæ, Goth. kniu, L. genu, Gr. γόνυ, Skr. jānu, √231. Cf. Genuflection.]

senses.d: To supplicate by kneeling.
q: Fall down, and knee The way into his mercy.

senses.d: To bend the knee; to fall or rest on the knees; — sometimes with down.
q: And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.
As soon as you are dressed, kneel and say the Lord's Prayer.

Kneel.etym: [OE. knelen, cneolien; akin to D. knielen, Dan. knæle. See Knee.]

senses.d: An instrument consisting of a thin blade, usually of steel and having a sharp edge for cutting, fastened to a handle, but of many different forms and names for different uses; as, table knife, drawing knife, putty knife, pallet knife, pocketknife, penknife, chopping knife, etc..
A sword or dagger.
q: The coward conquest of a wretch's knife.

Knife.etym: [OE. knif, AS. cnīf; akin to D. knijf, Icel. knīfr, Sw. knif, Dan. kniv.]

senses.d: To prune with the knife.
To cut or stab with a knife.
Fig.: To stab in the back; to try to defeat by underhand means, esp. in politics; to vote or work secretly against (a candidate of one's own party).
To form into a knot, or into knots; to tie together, as cord; to fasten by tying.
q: A great sheet knit at the four corners.
When your head did but ache, I knit my handkercher about your brows.

senses.d: To form, as a textile fabric, by the interlacing of yarn or thread in a series of connected loops, by means of needles, either by hand or by machinery; as, to knit stockings.
To join; to cause to grow together.
q: Nature can not knit the bones while the parts are under a discharge.

senses.d: To unite closely; to connect; to engage; as, hearts knit together in love.
q: Thy merit hath my duty strongly knit.
Come , knit hands, and beat the ground, In a light fantastic round.
A link among the days, toknit The generations each to each.

senses.d: To draw together; to contract into wrinkles.
q: He knits his brow and shows an angry eye.

Knit.etym: [OE. knitten, knutten, As. cnyttan, fr. cnotta knot; akin to Icel. kn�ta, Sw. knyta, Dan. knytte. See Knot.]

senses.d: To form a fabric by interlacing yarn or thread; to weave by making knots or loops.
To be united closely; to grow together; as, broken bones will in time knit and become sound.
Union knitting; texture.
of Knife. See Knife.
To drive or be driven against something; to strike against something; to clash; as, one heavy body knocks against another.
To strike or beat with something hard or heavy; to rap; as, to knock with a club; to knock on the door.
q: For harbor at a thousand doors they knocked.
Seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.

Knock.etym: [OE. knoken, AS. cnocian, cnucian; prob. of imitative origin; cf. Sw. knacka. Cf. Knack.]

senses.d: To strike with something hard or heavy; to move by striking; to drive (a thing) against something; as, to knock a ball with a bat; to knock the head against a post; to knock a lamp off the table.
q: When heroes knock their knotty heads together.

senses.d: To strike for admittance; to rap upon, as a door.
q: Master, knock the door hard.

senses.d: A blow; a stroke with something hard or heavy; a jar.
A stroke, as on a door for admittance; a rap.
q: A loud cry or some great knock.

senses.d: To practice evil speaking or fault-finding; to criticize habitually or captiously.
To impress strongly or forcibly; to astonish; to move to admiration or applause.
A beating; a rap; a series of raps.
q: The . . . repeated knockings of the head upon the ground by the Chinese worshiper.

senses.d: A knob; a bud; a bunch; a button.
q: Four bowls made like unto almonds, with their knops and their flowers.

senses.d: Any boldly projecting sculptured ornament; esp., the ornamental termination of a pinnacle, and then synonymous with finial; — called also knob, and knosp.

Knop.etym: [OE. knop, knoppe; cf. D. knop, knoop, G. knopf, Dan. knap, knop, Sw. knapp, knopp, button, bud, Icel. knappr, and E. knap, n. Cf. Knap, Knob.]

senses.d: Knee.
To perceive or apprehend clearly and certainly; to understand; to have full information of; as, to know one's duty.
q: O, that a man might know The end of this day's business ere it come!
There is a certainty in the proposition, and we know it.
Know how sublime a thing it is To suffer and be strong.

senses.d: To be convinced of the truth of; to be fully assured of; as, to know things from information.
To be acquainted with; to be no stranger to; to be more or less familiar with the person, character, etc., of; to possess experience of; as, to know an author; to know the rules of an organization.
q: He hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin.
Not to know me argues yourselves unknown.

senses.d: To recognize; to distinguish; to discern the character of; as, to know a person's face or figure.
q: Ye shall know them by their fruits.
And their eyes were opened, and they knew him.
To know Faithful friend from flattering foe.
At nearer view he thought he knew the dead.

senses.d: To have sexual commerce with.
q: And Adam knew Eve his wife.
And I knew that thou hearest me always.
The monk he instantly knew to be the prior.
In other hands I have known money do good.

Know.etym: [OE. knowen, knawen, AS. cnäwan; akin to OHG. chnäan (in comp.), Icel. knä to be able, Russ. znate to know, L. gnoscere, noscere, Gr. γιγηώσκειν, Skr. jnā; fr. the root of E. can, v. i., ken. √45. See Ken, Can to be able, and cf. Acquaint, Cognition, Gnome, Ignore, Noble, Note.]

senses.d: To have knowledge; to have a clear and certain perception; to possess wisdom, instruction, or information; — often with of.
q: Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider.
If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.
The peasant folklore of Europe still knows of willows that bleed and weep and speak when hewn.

senses.d: To be assured; to feel confident.
Skilful; well informed; intelligent; as, a knowing man; a knowing dog.
q: The knowing and intelligent part of the world.

senses.d: Artful; cunning; as, a knowing rascal.
Knowledge; hence, experience.
q: This sore night Hath trifled former knowings.

senses.d: The act or state of knowing; clear perception of fact, truth, or duty; certain apprehension; familiar cognizance; cognition.
q: Knowledge, which is the highest degree of the speculative faculties, consists in the perception of the truth of affirmative or negative propositions.

senses.d: That which is or may be known; the object of an act of knowing; a cognition; — chiefly used in the plural.
q: There is a great difference in the delivery of the mathematics, which are the most abstracted of knowledges.
Knowledges is a term in frequent use by Bacon, and, though now obsolete, should be revived, as without it we are compelled to borrow “cognitions” to express its import.
To use a word of Bacon's, now unfortunately obsolete, we must determine the relative value of knowledges.

senses.d: That which is gained and preserved by knowing; instruction; acquaintance; enlightenment; learning; scholarship; erudition.
q: Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Ignorance is the curse of God; Knowledge, the wing wherewith we fly to heaven.

senses.d: That familiarity which is gained by actual experience; practical skill; as, a knowledge of life.
q: Shipmen that had knowledge of the sea.

senses.d: Scope of information; cognizance; notice; as, it has not come to my knowledge.
q: Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldst take knowledge of me?

senses.d: Sexual intercourse; — usually preceded by carnal; as, carnal knowledge.

Knowledge.etym: [OE. knowlage, knowlege, knowleche, knawleche. The last part is the Icel. suffix -leikr, forming abstract nouns, orig. the same as Icel. leikr game, play, sport, akin to AS. lāc, Goth. laiks dance. See Know, and cf. Lake, v. i., Lark a frolic.]

senses.d: To acknowledge.
of Know.
